extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism students, and journalists interested in how routine news practices shape news content
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing how routine newsroom practices (beats, source routines, reporting methods) determine what becomes news and how it is framed; includes methods for investigating stories and critiques of ideological effects of newswork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat-based coverage / reliance on bureaucratic sources
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations cover the world mainly through 'beats,' which route reporters through governmental agencies and corporate bureaucracies and provide a predictable, steady flow of raw news material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters under daily deadlines come to depend upon these organizations for news; coverage organized by beats channels journalists to official sources and shapes what events are noticed and reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat round as a precondition of exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: The daily beat round—routine visits and contacts on assigned beats—is a primary mechanism determining reporters' exposure to events and information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The beat round structures what reporters see and learn; 'preconditions of exposure to the newsworld' means routines and access govern which happenings enter journalists' awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bureaucratic transformation of happenings into 'cases'
rubrics_metrics.description: Bureaucracies transform complex happenings into procedurally defined 'cases'; the information they produce represents their own bureaucratic reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because bureaucracies package events as cases, journalists who rely on them publicize that packaged reality as hard fact, marginalizing phenomena that do not fit bureaucratic phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonevents and what is ignored
rubrics_metrics.description: Occurrences that are not part of some bureaucratic phase are often ignored and thus do not become news—'nonevents' are a meaningful category in understanding news omissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attention to nonevents highlights how routine practices determine omissions: events outside bureaucratic channels or phase structures receive little coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of bureaucratic accounts as 'fact' vs other sources as unconfirmed
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists tend to treat accounts from official/bureaucratic sources as factual while regarding accounts from other sources as unconfirmed and requiring investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This asymmetry—'Fact' and bureaucratic accounts—explains why official perspectives are privileged; non-bureaucratic accounts face higher verification burdens and are less likely to be published quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for investigating and doubting accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: There are reasons for believing or doubting bureaucratic accounts; journalists must decide when to accept, when to investigate, and when to doubt official narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book discusses 'grounds for investigating the news' including criteria for believing bureaucratic accounts and markers that should prompt skepticism and further inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filling-in irregularities and missing information
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters routinely fill in irregularities and missing information when formulating stories; this 'filling-in' shapes the story's facts and narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irregularities and missing data are often resolved by reporters via available bureaucratic frames or assumptions—this practice affects accuracy and perspective in news reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspectival nature of events and fact-by-triangulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Events are perspectival; establishing 'facts' often involves triangulation—corroborating from multiple sources and perspectives rather than relying on a single account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book presents 'fact-by-triangulation' as a framework for news investigation and story formulation: using multiple vantage points to construct publishable facts while acknowledging perspective-dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: The practice and politics of newswork (news ideology and legitimation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine news practices produce ideological effects: news reports tend to support the interests of the status quo and legitimize prevailing political structures independent of individual reporters' intentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding 'news, ideology, and legitimation' requires examining sources of news ideology and the politics inherent in newswork; changing methods could produce different realities in the news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological approach to studying newswork (observation as apprentice/researcher)
rubrics_metrics.description: Studying newswork benefits from close observation—both as an apprentice and as a researcher—to capture routines, beat practices, and newsroom processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book's methodology sections ('Observations as an Apprentice' and 'Observations as a Researcher') suggest ethnographic/participant-observer techniques for understanding how news is produced in practice.
